name: Zygomatic arch reduction / reduction malarplasty
lead: Reduction malarplasty is a facial-bone surgery that narrows a wide or prominent cheekbone (zygoma) by cutting and repositioning the malar complex or zygomatic arch.[1][4] People have it to reduce bizygomatic width, soften a broad midface and obtain the slender, oval face that is considered attractive in East Asia.[8][9] Published authors describe it as one of the more commonly requested facial-contour procedures in East Asia and as rarely performed in the West.[1][3][10]

Techniques have evolved from coronal-incision approaches, which leave a scalp scar and carry facial-nerve risk, toward intraoral and limited-incision osteotomies.[2][3] The literature is made up of surgeon case series, technique descriptions and a 2023 systematic review of complications; randomized trials of the operation itself were not found.[11]

In looksmaxxing forums the term ZSO (zygomatic skeletal osteotomy) appears mostly in discussions about the opposite aim, projecting or repositioning cheekbones, and posters often compare it with malar implants and midface advancement.[7]
infobox: L-shaped, with plate or screw fixation[3][12]

paras: Reduction malarplasty is aimed at people with a wide bizygomatic width and a prominent zygomatic body or arch.[11] A review of cosmetic bone contouring notes that in some cultures a wide jaw and square face are viewed as less appealing, while an ovoid face is regarded as feminine and delicate, and that these procedures are requested increasingly in the United States as well as East Asia.[8] A Korean report states that prominent cheekbones in the Oriental physiognomy are linked in popular belief with bad luck and that a prominent zygoma can make a person look older and more stubborn, which patients may want to change.[9]

Wikipedia describes the assessment as based on an in-person examination plus photographs and X-ray or CT scans, with the three-quarter oblique view considered the most informative about projection; surgeons also assess skin thickness, since soft-tissue sagging after bone reduction is a recognised concern that may be addressed with lifting, buccal fat removal or fat grafting.[13] A 2022 review states that the size, contour and projection of the zygomaticomaxillary complex are sexually dimorphic and ethnically defined.[14]

An early technique used a coronal incision and either transposition osteoplasty of the malar complex or its removal and refixation.[1] Later authors described intraoral approaches intended to avoid visible scars, facial-nerve injury and long operative times.[2][4] A retrospective study of 418 cases reported an L-shaped osteotomy through an intraoral approach intended to allow control of the degree of reduction.[3] A percutaneous approach using small 3-mm incisions has also been described.[6]

Further variants include an L-shaped osteotomy through intraoral and sideburn incisions, in which two parallel horizontal cuts remove a middle segment of the anterior zygomatic body, the arch root is fractured through a small sideburn incision, and the freed complex is repositioned medially and fixed with one or two screws; in 32 patients the authors reported simple manipulation, stable fixation and less risk of a drooping face.[12] Other published options include an infracture technique with a short preauricular incision and a zygomatic arch-lifting technique.[16][17] A 2009 review of Asian aesthetic surgery stated that the popular choice for reduction malarplasty was to perform it safely via the intraoral approach.[10]
Wikipedia describes general anesthesia, double-bladed reciprocating saws and pre-bent titanium plates and screws as typical equipment.[13]

Zygomatic nonunion, in which the cut bone fails to heal, has been reported; one series of six patients attributed it to incomplete fixation in the narrow intraoral field and the pull of the masseter muscle.[5] The authors of intraoral and limited-incision methods cite scars and facial-nerve injury as drawbacks of coronal approaches.[2]

A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis covering 29 studies and 6,611 patients compared complications between techniques; it concluded that an L-shaped osteotomy without bone resection reduced the zygomatic complex with the lowest complication incidence, 0.02 percent, though the amount of reduction this allows is limited.[11] Case reports also describe sinusitis following the operation.[19] Wikipedia lists hematoma, swelling, numbness from infraorbital nerve involvement, asymmetry, infection and malunion among reported problems, with early numbness and swelling usually settling over about three to six months.[13]

Published human studies are retrospective surgical case series and technique reports, including a 418-case series from 2009 and a pooled analysis of 29 studies and 6,611 patients.[3][11] No randomized controlled trials of the operation have been found; one randomized trial concerned a training simulator for intraoral facial contouring surgery rather than patient outcomes.[20]

Reduction malarplasty was described in the early 1990s in the plastic surgery literature, with a coronal approach and osteoplasty, alongside a classification of prominent zygoma in Orientals.[1][21] Wikipedia credits Onizuka and colleagues with introducing an intraoral approach in 1983.[13] Through the late 1990s and 2000s surgeons published intraoral, preauricular and percutaneous alternatives, and a facelift combined with malar repositioning was also reported.[2][4][6][22]

A looksmax.org thread shows a user asking whether a ZSO or malarplasty with autologous bone would help the eye area, and a reply attributing flat cheekbones to a recessed maxilla and suggesting a LeFort III osteotomy instead.[7] This reflects a common forum framing in which cheek appearance is linked to midface projection.

card.summary: Cheekbone-narrowing osteotomy, mainly an East Asian aesthetic surgery, supported only by surgeon case series.
card.note: Major bone surgery with nerve injury and nonunion reported.

quick.overview:
Reduction malarplasty cuts and repositions the cheekbone to narrow a wide or prominent midface. Surgeons describe it as a commonly requested contouring procedure in East Asia.

The published literature is mostly retrospective case series and technique papers.
quick.mechanism: Osteotomies are made in the malar complex or zygomatic arch, through coronal, intraoral, preauricular or small percutaneous incisions, and the bone is repositioned or fixed.
quick.risks: Reported concerns include scars and facial-nerve injury with some approaches, and zygomatic nonunion after surgery. It is major surgery performed by trained surgeons.

chain: Osteotomy cuts the zygomatic body and arch
The freed cheekbone is moved inward and fixed with plates or screws
Bizygomatic width falls and the midface looks narrower and more oval
angle.text: Patients seeking a narrower, softer midface have the cheekbone cut and moved inward so the face is less wide in front and three-quarter views. Authors describe the goal as an oval or 'melon seed' contour rather than flattening the cheek.[8]
